definition: Inimical means hostile, harmful, or unfavorable in nature or effect, especially when describing conditions or surroundings.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word inimical. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know inimical should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The thin, dry air of the high desert proved inimical to the ferns, which shriveled within days of being planted there.
Unhelpful conditions merely fail to assist, while inimical conditions work against whatever is trying to survive in them.
Inimical conditions make survival difficult, but lethal ones kill outright.

Adverse means working against success or wellbeing, and it is the mild, official-sounding word - adverse weather, adverse effects. Inimical is stronger and more pointed: the conditions behave almost like an enemy of whatever tries to live or work in them. An adverse season sets the orchard back; an inimical climate means the orchard should never have been planted.

Hostile means unfriendly and actively opposed, and it attaches naturally to people and their intentions - a hostile crowd, a hostile takeover. Inimical does the same work for impersonal things: climates, chemistries, and policies that harm without meaning to. A hostile guard wants you gone; an inimical desert has no wants at all, yet works against you just the same.

Inimical means hostile, harmful, or unfavorable in nature or effect, especially when describing conditions or surroundings.
A grower planted a row of young lemon trees a hundred yards from a windy shoreline.
Salt spray coated the leaves at every high tide, and the sandy soil drained away every drop of fresh water within minutes.
Nothing at the site was obviously poisonous, yet not one tree ever put out healthy growth.
The conditions were simply inimical to citrus.
The site's conditions worked actively against the trees rather than merely failing to help them, which is what inimical describes.
formal, academic and scientific register

Inimical is nearly always followed by 'to' plus whatever is being harmed, as in 'inimical to plant growth' or 'inimical to open debate.' It usually describes conditions, climates, policies, or environments rather than a person's temperament; for an unfriendly person, plain 'hostile' is the better word.

Of all the planets our probes have visited, Venus guards itself most fiercely.
The Soviet landers of the 1970s and 80s were engineering marvels, armored like submarines, yet none survived on the surface for much more than two hours.

An environment of crushing pressure, sulfuric clouds, and lead-melting heat is not merely difficult; it is actively inimical to machinery, corroding circuits and buckling hulls with no malice and no pause.
Engineers sometimes joke that Venus does not resist visitors so much as digest them.
Newer mission designs accept the verdict: instead of toughening landers further, they aim for the calmer clouds fifty kilometers up, where the planet stops behaving like an enemy.
